opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot. In computational biology there's a real tension. On one hand, we have decades of accumulated knowledge: pathways, gene regulatory networks, protein interactions, curated annotations. It seems wasteful not to use that. On the other hand, if you lean on it too heavily, you only find what you already expected, and you lose the chance to discover something new.

My view is that prior knowledge should guide the model, not constrain it. Biological datasets, especially high-dimensional ones like gene expression, typically have far more features than samples. With twenty thousand genes and a few hundred patients, a purely data-driven model will pick up spurious patterns. Prior knowledge works as a regularizer. For example, you can encourage genes known to work together in a pathway to have similar effects, or give certain features a higher prior probability of being important. That makes the results more statistically stable and easier for biologists to interpret.

But I strongly prefer approaches where the data can override the prior when the evidence is strong. Our knowledge bases are incomplete and biased toward well-studied genes and diseases. If a model hard-codes them, it inherits those biases. So we try to build models where you can see how much the result depends on the prior versus the data. That leads to something I care about a lot, which is explainability.

Once you have a flexible model, even a complex deep learning model, you can use explanation methods afterward to ask which features drove a prediction. Then you can compare those explanations against prior knowledge. When they agree, that's reassuring, a kind of sanity check that the model learned something biologically meaningful. When they disagree, that's often the most interesting part. Either the model is exploiting an artifact like a batch effect, which you want to catch, or it's pointing to a new biological hypothesis worth testing experimentally.

So in short, I see prior knowledge playing two roles. It can be built in softly to make learning feasible from limited samples. And it can serve as a reference point for validating and interpreting what the model learned. The goal isn't to confirm textbooks but to use them as a starting point, so that a model's departures from them become real discoveries rather than noise.

r001.rationale: The response says prior knowledge should guide the model rather than constrain it, and that data should be able to override the prior when evidence is strong.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, it's great to be here. That's a question I think about a lot, because it sits right at the center of what my lab does.

My short answer is that prior knowledge should be used, but it should be used carefully, and it should never be allowed to override what the data is actually telling you. Biology is a field where we have accumulated decades of hard-won knowledge: pathway databases, protein interaction networks, gene ontology annotations, known regulatory relationships. It would be wasteful to throw all of that away and pretend every new dataset is a blank slate. At the same time, that knowledge is incomplete, it's biased toward what has been well studied, and some of it is simply wrong. So if you bake it in too rigidly, you end up rediscovering what you already believed and missing the genuinely new biology.

The way I like to think about it is that prior knowledge should shape the hypothesis space rather than dictate the answer. For example, in a lot of our work on interpretable machine learning for genomics and clinical data, we use known pathways or network structure as a kind of soft constraint. A model might be encouraged to explain a phenotype in terms of gene sets that make biological sense, but it still has the freedom to deviate when the data strongly supports something outside those sets. That tends to give you two benefits at once. You get better statistical power, because you're borrowing strength across genes that are known to act together, and you get explanations that a biologist can actually read and act on.

The second thing I'd emphasize is that prior knowledge is especially valuable on the interpretation side, not just the modeling side. A lot of my work has been on feature attribution methods like SHAP, where you ask a model which inputs drove a particular prediction. If you take those attributions and look at them gene by gene, you often get noise. If you aggregate them through pathways or through known biological structure, you start to see coherent stories, and you can also spot when the model is latching onto something that looks like an artifact, like a batch effect or a hospital-specific coding pattern in clinical data.

And that leads to the third point, which is that the relationship should go both ways. The data should also be allowed to challenge and update the prior knowledge. Some of the most interesting results we've had came from cases where the model consistently pointed at genes or interactions that weren't in any database, and when collaborators followed up experimentally, it turned out there was real biology there. If we had hard-coded the known network, we would never have seen that.

So to summarize: use prior knowledge to regularize and to interpret, keep it soft enough that the data can push back, and treat disagreements between the two as the most interesting places to look rather than as errors to be smoothed away.

r001.rationale: The response says prior knowledge should shape the hypothesis space without dictating the answer, and that data must be able to challenge it. This clearly communicates that methods should not depend entirely on prior knowledge.

astra-6.text:
I think prior knowledge is very valuable, but we have to be careful about how we use it. In biology, what we know is incomplete, and some genes and pathways have been studied much more extensively than others. If we build those assumptions too strongly into a method, we may end up rediscovering what we already know and missing something unexpected.

So I like to distinguish using prior knowledge to guide learning from using it to interpret and validate what we find. For example, we can ask whether a pattern learned from the data is consistent with known biology, but we should also leave room for patterns that aren’t explained by existing knowledge. Those could reflect noise or confounding, but they could also point to new biology.

The important thing is to be clear about what came from the data and what we put into the model. Agreement with prior knowledge isn’t independent validation if that same knowledge was used to produce the result. Ultimately, we want methods that benefit from what we know while still allowing us to discover what we don’t.

r001.rationale: The response says prior knowledge should guide methods without being built in so strongly that they miss unexpected patterns, and that methods should still allow discovery beyond what is already known.

sol-6.1.text:
I think prior knowledge is very valuable, but we have to be careful about where we put it in the analysis. If we constrain a model to find only relationships that are already in a pathway database, for example, we may miss precisely the biology that we’re trying to discover. Those databases are incomplete, and some parts of biology have been studied much more than others.

So I like to give the data an opportunity to tell us something new, and then use prior knowledge to help interpret and validate what we find. Does a result agree with an established mechanism? If it doesn’t, is it an artifact, or is it a hypothesis worth testing experimentally? The goal is to benefit from what we already know without making that knowledge the boundary of what we can discover.

r001.rationale: The response says prior knowledge should help interpret and validate findings, but should not constrain discovery; it gives the data an opportunity to reveal new biology.
